n: A message against the Philistines, Israel’s ancient coastal rivals, given before a Pharaoh attacked Gaza. Which Pharaoh and when is uncertain—possibly Necho around 609 BC.

f.g: A people who settled on the southern coast of Canaan around 1200 BC; the name “Palestine” comes from them.
The southernmost of the five main Philistine cities.

n: Waters are rising from the north—an image of Babylon’s army sweeping in like a river in flood, drowning towns and people. Everyone cries and wails.

f.w: waters rise up out of the north

n: At the thunder of galloping horses and rumbling chariot wheels, fathers are so paralyzed with fear they don’t even turn back to help their children.
The day has come to destroy the Philistines and cut off Tyre and Sidon’s last allies. The Philistines are the “remnant of Caphtor,” their ancestral island home.

f.g: Usually identified with Crete or the Aegean region, from which the Philistines came.
Phoenician cities that may have been allied with the Philistines.

n: Gaza shaves its head in mourning; Ashkelon is silenced. How long will you gash yourselves in grief?

f.g: Shaving the head was a sign of mourning.
Cutting the body was a pagan mourning rite.
Nebuchadnezzar destroyed Ashkelon in 604 BC; archaeologists have found its destruction layer.

n: Someone cries out: “Sword of the Lord, how long until you rest? Go back into your sheath and be still!”

f.w: O thou sword of the LORD

n: The answer: how can it rest when the Lord has given it orders against Ashkelon and the coast? Babylon’s sword moves only under God’s command.
